reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours of the CNS
clinicalPearls: A benign neuronal tumour (CNS WHO grade 1) composed of mature but dysplastic ganglion (neuronal) cells without a neoplastic glial component
Distinguished from ganglioglioma by the absence of a neoplastic glial element
Often cortical and supratentorial, and a recognised cause of chronic focal epilepsy
The cerebellar variant, dysplastic cerebellar gangliocytoma (Lhermitte-Duclos disease), is associated with germline PTEN mutation and Cowden syndrome
MRI usually shows a well-circumscribed, sometimes calcified lesion; the cerebellar variant has a characteristic striated 'tigroid' folial pattern
Surgical resection is generally curative for the typical cortical tumour
Recognition of the cerebellar variant should prompt evaluation for Cowden syndrome and its associated cancer risks
reference.pathophysiology: Gangliocytoma is a benign neuronal tumour formed of clusters of mature but dysplastic ganglion cells set in a stroma of non-neoplastic glial tissue, differing from ganglioglioma in that the glial component is not itself neoplastic. It commonly arises in the cerebral cortex and, when supratentorial, disrupts local circuitry to produce focal epilepsy. The distinctive cerebellar variant, dysplastic cerebellar gangliocytoma or Lhermitte-Duclos disease, consists of hypertrophic dysplastic ganglion cells expanding the cerebellar folia and is strongly linked to germline PTEN mutation as part of Cowden syndrome, a phakomatosis with increased risk of breast, thyroid and other tumours. Growth is slow and the lesions are essentially non-progressive.
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI to characterise the lesion, including the striated folial pattern of the cerebellar variant
Video-EEG when the tumour presents with focal epilepsy
Histopathology showing dysplastic ganglion cells without a neoplastic glial component
PTEN germline testing when the cerebellar variant or Cowden features are present
Screening for Cowden syndrome-associated tumours (breast, thyroid, endometrium)
Neuropsychological assessment as part of epilepsy surgery evaluation
redFlags: Drug-resistant seizures affecting quality of life
Cerebellar variant causing mass effect, ataxia or obstructive hydrocephalus
Features suggesting Cowden syndrome with heightened systemic cancer risk
Atypical growth or enhancement suggesting an alternative diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is excellent, as gangliocytoma is benign and slow-growing; complete resection of a symptomatic cortical tumour is usually curative. The cerebellar variant may recur if incompletely removed, and its main long-term significance lies in the associated Cowden syndrome and lifelong surveillance for related cancers.
pitfalls: Confusing gangliocytoma with ganglioglioma and misjudging the presence of a neoplastic glial component
Failing to test for germline PTEN and diagnose Cowden syndrome in the cerebellar variant
Overlooking the diagnosis in long-standing focal epilepsy
Incomplete resection of the cerebellar lesion leading to recurrence
references: WHO Classification of Tumours of the Central Nervous System
Louis DN et al. The 2021 WHO Classification of Tumors of the Central Nervous System
management: Surgical resection is the mainstay and is usually curative for the typical cortical tumour
For tumours presenting with focal epilepsy, pursue an epilepsy-surgery evaluation with video-EEG and neuropsychological assessment, aiming for seizure freedom
Control seizures with antiepileptic drugs pending or alongside surgery
For the cerebellar variant (Lhermitte-Duclos disease), resect symptomatic lesions causing mass effect or hydrocephalus
Undertake surveillance MRI to detect residual or recurrent disease, particularly after incomplete cerebellar resection
Test for germline PTEN mutation when the cerebellar variant or Cowden features are present, with lifelong surveillance for breast, thyroid and endometrial tumours
Offer genetic counselling and family screening where Cowden syndrome is confirmed
